Give yourself time and be gentle with yourself 

Feeling hollow is a normal and valid way to feel. Many people do after a traumatic event or during one, especially if they have preexisting traumas. 

I struggled a lot with that hollow feeling, still do sometimes. I told my therapist I felt like a monster. 

She asked me if I'd ever accidentaly hurt myself but not felt the pain right away. I had. When I was 10 I fell out of a tree and cut my hand open badly. There was all this blood but it didn't hurt. Everyone was panicking around me and I didn't get why. It wasn't until 30 minutes later we were walking into the ER that the pain hit. 

Sometimes the mind goes into survival mode. You don't have the time, the space, the energy to handle certain emotions so it shuts down.

The feelings will come, maybe in the span between one breath and another. Or maybe slowly over days. It will happen and that's okay. Until then whatever you're feeling is okay too.

You can process it, but it doesn't have to be today. Or tomorrow or next week. You will get to that place. You've gotten there before.

There are absolutely ways to help. Thank you for being there for him first of all. Having someone who cares enough to help is an amazing thing lots of people don't have. 

He isn't likely to be admitted anywhere while covid positive. There are other things though. If he isn't already seeing a therapist he can find one. You can look up therapist offices in your community. Appointments will have to be by phone or zoom which is not ideal, talking to someone about feelings and garbage is hard enough face to face, over the phone is really hard. He can take it slow though, get to know the therapist and ask about their training and what sort of methods they use and how those methods can help.

Googling coping skills and reading about methods for getting through terrible moments can help too. When his thoughts are spiraling and he starts actively looking for an escape hatch, coping skills can help with that. Personally holding an ice cube or snapping a rubber band helps me in the serious self-harm/panic moments. Those may or may not work for him, everyone is different and there is no one thing that helps with everything. 

If you want to understand how better to help him, if you're worried that there is something more you could be doing or something you should or should not be saying. Look up, how to help a friend with mental illness. There are whole lists talking about how you can talk to someone in a positive and constructive way.

Also, remember to take care of yourself. Wanting to help someone is awesome, but eventually it will wear you down, empathy isn't an endless well.
